title: Τηλεμάχου ἀπόπλους
about: Mocked once more by the suitors, Telemachus goes down to his father's storeroom and has the old nurse Eurycleia provision a ship in secret, swearing her to silence and comforting her fear with the assurance that a god stands behind his plan. That night Athena, disguised first as Telemachus and then as Mentor, gathers a crew, borrows a ship from Noemon, lulls the suitors to sleep, and leads Telemachus down to the harbor, where the ship sails out under a favoring wind toward Pylos.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐκ χειρὸς χεῖρα σπάσατ’ Ἀντινόοιο
ῥεῖα·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and out of his hand drew his hand, Antinous's,
easily;
sentences.i: So he said, and easily drew his hand from Antinous's;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα closes direct speech before the narrative resumes: ἦ is the unaugmented 3 sg. of ἠμί 'say' — this part opens mid-scene, continuing Telemachus's rebuff of Antinous — and ῥα is the enclitic ἄρα 'then, so'. σπάσατ' is σπάσατο, the aorist middle of σπάω 'draw, pull', with no augment: Homer's past tenses regularly drop the ε-, a pattern flagged here once for the whole part. ἐκ χειρὸς ... Ἀντινόοιο shows hyperbaton: the genitive Ἀντινόοιο 'Antinous's' belongs with χειρός but is held to the line's end, separated from it by the accusative χεῖρα 'his own hand', and is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου), the ending noted throughout this part. ῥεῖα 'easily' opens line 322 to complete the sentence.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δὲ δόμον κάτα δαῖτα πένοντο.
sentences.l: but the suitors, throughout the house, at the feast were busy.
sentences.i: but the suitors, all through the house, went on with their feasting.
sentences.n: κάτα is anastrophe: the preposition follows its noun, δόμον κάτα = κατὰ δόμον 'throughout the house', and its accent shifts back onto the first syllable, a pattern also seen with βοῦς and similar nouns. δαῖτα is the accusative of δαίς 'feast, meal', governed by πένοντο, the middle of πένομαι 'labor at, be busy with'. δέ marks the shift back to the ordinary suitors after Antinous's rebuff.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπελώβευον καὶ ἐκερτόμεον ἐπέεσσιν.
sentences.l: and they kept mocking and taunting him with words.
sentences.i: and they went on mocking and taunting him with their words.
sentences.n: ἐπελώβευον (from ἐπιλωβεύομαι, 'heap outrage upon', a rare compound of λώβη 'outrage, insult') and ἐκερτόμεον (from κερτομέω 'taunt, jeer at') are imperfects, casting the suitors' mockery as a continuing scene rather than a single act. ἐπέεσσιν is a dative plural of ἔπος 'word' in -εσσι(ν) (Attic ἔπεσι), one of the long Homeric dative endings that recur throughout this part. οἱ is the pronoun 'they' — in Homer the word later used as the definite article regularly still works as a plain personal pronoun, as here.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: and one of the overbearing young men would say something like this:
sentences.n: εἴπεσκε is an iterative imperfect, formed with the suffix -σκε added to the aorist stem εἰπ-: 'would say, used to say', marking a repeated, typical taunt rather than a single remark — this -σκε iterative recurs at 331 and has no Attic equivalent. τις is the indefinite pronoun, 'someone, one of them'. ὑπερηνορεόντων is the genitive plural of the present participle of ὑπερηνορέω, 'play the overbearing man' (built on ἀνήρ 'man' with the prefix ὑπερ- 'over, beyond'), partitive with τις. It is uncontracted (-εόντων, not -οῦντων), one of several such Homeric forms in this part.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα Τηλέμαχος φόνον ἡμῖν μερμηρίζει.
sentences.l: Truly indeed Telemachus is devising murder against us.
sentences.i: Telemachus is surely plotting murder against us.
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα is an emphatic opening, 'truly, indeed'. μερμηρίζει, from μερμηρίζω 'ponder anxiously, devise', takes φόνον as its object and ἡμῖν as a dative of disadvantage, 'against us'. This is the first of two anonymous suitors' speeches in this part (the second follows at 331); Murray names neither speaker, marking the suitors here only as a faceless, mocking crowd.

sentences.t:
ἤ τινας ἐκ Πύλου ἄξει ἀμύντορας ἠμαθόεντος
ἢ ὅ γε καὶ Σπάρτηθεν, ἐπεί νύ περ ἵεται αἰνῶς·
sentences.l:
Either some helpers from sandy Pylos he will bring,
or he himself also from Sparta, since indeed he is terribly eager;
sentences.i: Either he will bring some champions from sandy Pylos, or he himself will go even from Sparta, so terribly set is he on it;
sentences.n: ἀμύντορας is the accusative plural of ἀμύντωρ 'defender, helper' (from ἀμύνω 'ward off'). ἠμαθόεντος, genitive of ἠμαθόεις 'sandy', keeps Pylos's fixed epithet in an oblique case (compare Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα, the accusative already fixed as 'sandy Pylos'). Σπάρτηθεν carries the suffix -θεν 'from', one of the directional suffixes (with -δε 'to' and -θι 'at') that recur through this part. ὅ γε is the pronoun 'he', emphatic with γε. ἵεται is the middle of ἵημι, here 'is eager, presses on', with the adverb αἰνῶς 'terribly' and the particles νύ περ adding emphasis to the suitor's alarm.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ καὶ εἰς Ἐφύρην ἐθέλει, πίειραν ἄρουραν,
ἐλθεῖν, ὄφρ’ ἔνθεν θυμοφθόρα φάρμακ’ ἐνείκῃ,
ἐν δὲ βάλῃ κρητῆρι καὶ ἡμέας πάντας ὀλέσσῃ.
sentences.l:
Or even to Ephyra he wishes, the fertile plowland,
to go, so that from there heart-destroying drugs he may bring,
and cast them into the mixing-bowl and destroy all of us.
sentences.i: Or perhaps he means to go to Ephyra, that rich land, to fetch deadly poison from there, and put it in the mixing-bowl and destroy us all.
sentences.n: ἐθέλει ... ἐλθεῖν has the infinitive thrown across the line-break, apart from the verb it completes, a common Homeric enjambment. πίειραν ἄρουραν 'a fat plowland' stands in apposition to Ἐφύρην. ἐν δὲ βάλῃ is tmesis for ἐμβάλῃ 'cast in': the preverb ἐν stands apart from its verb βάλῃ, an aorist subjunctive after ὄφρα expressing purpose, as is ἐνείκῃ (from the defective verb behind ἐνεγκεῖν, 'carry, bring'). θυμοφθόρα φάρμακα 'heart-destroying drugs' names the deadly potions for which Ephyra was known.

sentences.t: ἄλλος δ’ αὖτ’ εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: But another, in turn, would say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: But another of the overbearing young men would say in his turn:
sentences.n: The line repeats 324 with ἄλλος αὖτε 'another, in turn' replacing ὧδέ τις, introducing a second, equally anonymous speaker. εἴπεσκε is again the iterative imperfect in -σκε (see 324); ὑπερηνορεόντων is the same uncontracted participle.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ οἶδ’, εἴ κε καὶ αὐτὸς ἰὼν κοίλης ἐπὶ νηὸς
τῆλε φίλων ἀπόληται ἀλώμενος ὥς περ Ὀδυσσεύς;
sentences.l:
And who knows if he himself too, going aboard a hollow ship,
far from his dear ones may perish, wandering, just as Odysseus?
sentences.i: And who knows whether he too, going aboard a hollow ship, may perish far from his own people, wandering just as Odysseus did?
sentences.n: τίς δ' οἶδ(ε) is a common Homeric turn, 'and who knows...', introducing a genuinely open possibility. οἶδε is a perfect with present force, 'knows'. εἴ κε with the subjunctive ἀπόληται is a vivid future condition, 'if he should perish'; κε here is the epic equivalent of ἄν, one of the small particles (with ῥα, ἄρ, νυ, περ) that recur throughout Homer. τῆλε φίλων is a genitive of separation, 'far from his own people'. κοίλης ἐπὶ νηός, 'aboard a hollow ship', echoes the house-fixed plural κοῖλαι νῆες in the singular. ἀλώμενος, the present participle of ἀλάομαι 'wander', is applied here to Telemachus by comparison with Odysseus, whose own wandering is named explicitly in the words that follow, ὥς περ Ὀδυσσεύς 'just as Odysseus'.

sentences.t: οὕτω κεν καὶ μᾶλλον ὀφέλλειεν πόνον ἄμμιν·
sentences.l: Thus indeed even more would he increase toil for us;
sentences.i: That would only add all the more to our trouble;
sentences.n: ὀφέλλειεν is the optative of ὀφέλλω 'increase, augment' (not to be confused with ὀφείλω 'owe', a common confusion since both give similar-looking forms); with κεν it is a potential optative, 'would increase'. ἄμμιν is the epic dative plural of the first-person pronoun (= ἡμῖν), built on the stem ἄμμε seen also in ἄμμες.

sentences.t:
κτήματα γάρ κεν πάντα δασαίμεθα, οἰκία δ’ αὖτε
τούτου μητέρι δοῖμεν ἔχειν ἠδ’ ὅς τις ὀπυίοι.
sentences.l:
For his possessions all we would divide amongst us, but the house, in turn,
to this man's mother we would give to keep, and to whoever should marry her.
sentences.i: We would divide up all his goods among us, and give the house, in turn, to his mother to keep — and to whichever man should marry her.
sentences.n: δασαίμεθα (from δατέομαι 'divide, share out') and δοῖμεν (from δίδωμι) are both optatives in the potential sense governed by the same κεν of line 334, 'we would...'. τούτου is the demonstrative pronoun, 'of this man', referring contemptuously to Telemachus. ὀπυίοι is a potential optative in a relative clause with indefinite force, 'whoever might marry her' — the suitors are already imagining Penelope remarried and the house divided.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάν, ὁ δ’ ὑψόροφον θάλαμον κατεβήσετο πατρὸς
εὐρύν, ὅθι νητὸς χρυσὸς καὶ χαλκὸς ἔκειτο
ἐσθής τ’ ἐν χηλοῖσιν ἅλις τ’ ἐυῶδες ἔλαιον·
sentences.i: So they said; and he went down into his father's high-roofed chamber, a wide room where heaped gold and bronze lay stored, and clothing in chests, and abundant sweet-smelling oil;
sentences.n: φάν is φάσαν/ἔφασαν, the unaugmented 3rd plural imperfect of φημί, 'they said' — closing both anonymous taunts at once. ὁ δέ, 'but he', is the pronoun again, now Telemachus. εὐρύν, agreeing with θάλαμον, is held over to the start of line 338, separated from its noun by the intervening ὑψόροφον, a common Homeric hyperbaton. νητός is a verbal adjective of νέω 'heap up, pile', describing treasure stored away. ἐσθής, ἐν χηλοῖσιν and ἅλις ἐυῶδες ἔλαιον form a brief inventory of the household's stored wealth, the treasury a great house would keep for its master's use.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ πίθοι οἴνοιο παλαιοῦ ἡδυπότοιο
ἕστασαν, ἄκρητον θεῖον ποτὸν ἐντὸς ἔχοντες,
ἑξείης ποτὶ τοῖχον ἀρηρότες, εἴ ποτ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
οἴκαδε νοστήσειε καὶ ἄλγεα πολλὰ μογήσας.
sentences.l:
And within, jars of wine, old and sweet to drink,
were standing, holding within unmixed, divine drink,
fitted in a row against the wall, in case ever Odysseus
should come home, and having suffered many pains.
sentences.i: and inside stood jars of wine, old and sweet to drink, holding the strong, unmixed liquor within, ranged in a row along the wall, kept there in case Odysseus should ever come home again, after all his many sufferings.
sentences.n: ἕστασαν is a pluperfect of ἵστημι used with simple past force, 'were standing', built by reduplication (ἑ-στα-σαν) rather than an ordinary augment. οἴνοιο and ἡδυπότοιο are genitives in -οιο, Homer's regular ending for the second declension (= Attic -ου). ἄκρητον 'unmixed' describes wine drunk without the water Greeks ordinarily added; θεῖον ποτόν 'divine drink' marks its potency. ἀρηρότες is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together, join', here 'ranged closely'. οἴκαδε carries the directional suffix -δε, 'homeward' (with -θεν 'from' and -θι 'at', the set of place-suffixes noted throughout this part). νοστήσειε is an optative of hope or expectation, 'should he ever return' — the storeroom is being kept ready against the day of the master's return.

sentences.t:
κληισταὶ δ’ ἔπεσαν σανίδες πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαι,
δικλίδες·
sentences.l:
And close-fitting boards were shut fast, closely fitted,
folding-doors;
sentences.i: Close-fitting doors, folding shut and tightly joined, closed off the room;
sentences.n: ἔπεσαν, from πίπτω, is used here in its idiomatic sense 'fell to, closed', of a door swinging shut, rather than 'fell down'. ἀραρυῖαι is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together, join' (as ἀρηρότες was at 342, masculine there and feminine here, agreeing with σανίδες 'boards, door-leaves'), πυκινῶς 'closely, snugly'. δικλίδες, 'double, folding', describes a door hung in two leaves, the ordinary arrangement for a storeroom that needed to be sealed against a large space.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ γυνὴ ταμίη νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ
ἔσχ’, ἣ πάντ’ ἐφύλασσε νόου πολυϊδρείῃσιν,
Εὐρύκλει’, Ὦπος θυγάτηρ Πεισηνορίδαο.
sentences.l:
and within, a woman, a housekeeper, night and day
had charge of it, who guarded everything with the many wisdoms of her mind,
Eurycleia, Ops’ daughter, Peisenor’s grandson.
sentences.i: and inside, a woman, the housekeeper, had charge of it night and day, watching over everything with the shrewdness of her mind — Eurycleia, daughter of Ops son of Peisenor.
sentences.n: ταμίη 'housekeeper, stewardess' will later take the fixed epithet αἰδοίη 'revered'; here Murray gives her none yet. νόου πολυϊδρείῃσιν is an instrumental dative plural in -ῃσι (Attic -αις) with πολυϊδρείη 'much cunning, shrewdness'. Εὐρύκλει', Ὦπος θυγάτηρ Πεισηνορίδαο is a line identical to one already published in odyssey-004 (1.428), and its l is reused verbatim there, including its rendering of Πεισηνορίδαο as 'Peisenor's grandson' — strictly, since Πεισηνορίδης 'son of Peisenor' agrees with Ὦψ, the sense is that Ops was Peisenor's son (making Eurycleia his granddaughter, not grandson); the shipped wording is kept as the repeated-line rule requires, and the discrepancy is flagged here rather than silently corrected. The published i for the same line correctly gives 'daughter of Ops son of Peisenor', which is followed here for i.

sentences.t: τὴν τότε Τηλέμαχος προσέφη θαλαμόνδε καλέσσας·
sentences.l: Her then Telemachus addressed, to the chamber having called her:
sentences.i: Telemachus then called her to the chamber and spoke to her:
sentences.n: τήν is the pronoun object, 'her', anticipating Εὐρύκλεια. θαλαμόνδε carries the directional suffix -δε again ('to the chamber', as οἴκαδε at 343). καλέσσας is the aorist participle of καλέω with the epic double σ, 'having called'. This narrator's line introduces Telemachus's instructions to Eurycleia that follow.

sentences.t:
μαῖ’, ἄγε δή μοι οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν ἄφυσσον
ἡδύν, ὅτις μετὰ τὸν λαρώτατος ὃν σὺ φυλάσσεις
κεῖνον ὀιομένη τὸν κάμμορον, εἴ ποθεν ἔλθοι
διογενὴς Ὀδυσεὺς θάνατον καὶ κῆρας ἀλύξας.
sentences.l:
Nurse, come now, for me wine in jars draw off,
the sweet, which after that one is most delicious, which you are guarding,
that one expecting, the ill-fated, if from somewhere he should come,
Zeus-sprung Odysseus, death and the fates having escaped.
sentences.i: Nurse, come now, draw off wine for me into jars — the sweet wine, the best after the one you are keeping in reserve for that ill-fated man, in case he should come from somewhere, Zeus-born Odysseus, having escaped death and the fates of death.
sentences.n: μαῖα is an affectionate term of address for an old nurse, here vocative μαῖ'. ἄφυσσον, imperative of ἀφύσσω 'draw off, ladle', governs οἶνον; ἡδύν 'sweet' is thrown to the head of the next line, away from its noun, a hyperbaton like εὐρύν at 338. λαρώτατος is a superlative of λαρός 'pleasant to the taste'. ὀιομένη, from ὀίομαι 'suppose, expect', explains the reserved wine: Eurycleia has kept her best vintage in hope of Odysseus's return. διογενής, 'sprung from Zeus', is a new fixed epithet here, kept distinct from δῖος 'heavenly' and θεοειδής 'godlike in form' (see new-renderings.md); it recurs at 366. κῆρες are the spirits of death (from κήρ), often paired with θάνατος as a doublet. ἀλύξας is the aorist participle of ἀλύσκω 'escape'.

sentences.t: δώδεκα δ’ ἔμπλησον καὶ πώμασιν ἄρσον ἅπαντας.
sentences.l: And twelve fill up, and with covers fit them all.
sentences.i: Fill twelve jars, and fit them all with lids.
sentences.n: ἔμπλησον is the aorist imperative of ἐμπίμπλημι 'fill up'. ἄρσον is the aorist imperative of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together, join' (the same verb behind ἀρηρότες at 342 and ἀραρυῖαι at 344), here 'fasten' with πώμασιν, the dative plural of πῶμα 'lid, cover'. δώδεκα, 'twelve', understands ἀμφιφορεῖς 'jars' from the line before.

sentences.t: ἐν δέ μοι ἄλφιτα χεῦον ἐϋρραφέεσσι δοροῖσιν·
sentences.l: And in for me barley-meal pour, into well-sewn skin-bags;
sentences.i: And pour barley-meal for me into well-stitched leather bags;
sentences.n: ἐν ... χεῦον is tmesis for ἔγχεον, the preverb ἐν standing apart from the imperative χεῦον (aorist of χέω 'pour'). δοροῖσιν, dative plural of δορός 'skin, hide, leather sack' (Attic δορά), is in the Homeric ending -οισι(ν). ἐϋρραφέεσσι, an uncontracted dative plural of ἐϋρραφής 'well-stitched' (ἐϋ- + ῥάπτω 'sew'), is repeated at 380 of the same bags.

sentences.t: εἴκοσι δ’ ἔστω μέτρα μυληφάτου ἀλφίτου ἀκτῆς.
sentences.l: And twenty let there be, measures of mill-ground barley grain.
sentences.i: And let there be twenty measures of barley-meal ground at the mill.
sentences.n: ἔστω is the 3rd singular imperative of εἰμί, 'let there be'. ἀκτή here is not the common word 'shore' but a separate epic noun meaning 'grain, meal' — the two are homonyms, and only context (μυληφάτου ἀλφίτου, 'of mill-ground barley') shows which is meant. μυληφάτου is a compound of μύλη 'mill' and a verbal element meaning 'struck, ground'.

sentences.t: αὐτὴ δ’ οἴη ἴσθι·
sentences.l: But know it, you yourself, alone;
sentences.i: But you alone are to know of this;
sentences.n: ἴσθι is ambiguous in form between the imperative of εἰμί 'be!' and that of οἶδα 'know!'; the sense here, confirmed by the parallel at 412 (μία δ' οἴη μῦθον ἄκουσεν, 'she alone heard of it'), is 'know it, you alone' — Telemachus swears Eurycleia to secrecy before he has even asked for her oath. αὐτὴ ... οἴη doubles the emphasis on her being the only one entrusted.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ ἁθρόα πάντα τετύχθω·
sentences.l: and let all these things, in a mass, be made ready;
sentences.i: and let it all be got ready together;
sentences.n: τετύχθω is a perfect passive imperative of τεύχω 'make, prepare', 'let it stand accomplished'; ἁθρόα 'all together, in a body' is the same word this part already used of the treasure stored in heaps (337–339) and will use again of the gathered comrades (392) and the assembled provisions (411). τά is the pronoun again, referring back to the wine and meal just ordered.

sentences.t:
ἑσπέριος γὰρ ἐγὼν αἱρήσομαι, ὁππότε κεν δὴ
μήτηρ εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβῇ κοίτου τε μέδηται.
sentences.l:
For in the evening I myself will take it, whenever indeed
my mother to her upper chamber goes up and of her bed takes thought.
sentences.i: for I will come for it myself in the evening, once my mother has gone up to her room and turns her thoughts to sleep.
sentences.n: ἑσπέριος is an adjective used adverbially, 'at evening'. ὁππότε κεν with the subjunctive ἀναβῇ (from ἀναβαίνω) is a general temporal clause, 'whenever'; κεν again stands for ἄν. μέδηται, from μέδομαι 'be mindful of, plan', takes the genitive κοίτου 'of rest, of going to bed'. ὑπερῷον is the women's upper chamber, where Penelope regularly withdraws in this poem.

sentences.t:
εἶμι γὰρ ἐς Σπάρτην τε καὶ ἐς Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα
νόστον πευσόμενος πατρὸς φίλου, ἤν που ἀκούσω.
sentences.l:
for I go to Sparta and to sandy Pylos,
of my dear father's homecoming to inquire, if perhaps somewhere I may hear.
sentences.i: for I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to ask after the homecoming of my dear father, in case I may hear something of him somewhere.
sentences.n: εἶμι γὰρ ἐς Σπάρτην τε καὶ ἐς Πύλον ἠμαθόεντα repeats word for word the line already published at 2.214 (odyssey-007), and its l ('for I go to Sparta and to sandy Pylos,') is reused here unchanged; the line that follows there differs from this one (πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο there, πατρὸς φίλου here), so only the shared line keeps its shipped wording. πευσόμενος is a future participle of purpose from πυνθάνομαι 'inquire, learn by asking'; φίλου with πατρός is the weakened sense of φίλος as a simple possessive, 'my own father'. ἤν is the epic form of ἐάν, and που is 'somewhere, perhaps'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, κώκυσεν δὲ φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια,
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and cried out his dear nurse Eurycleia,
and, lamenting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his dear nurse Eurycleia cried out, and, lamenting, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the fixed closing formula for a speech, kept as 'So he spoke' throughout. κώκυσεν, from κωκύω, is a sharper cry of grief than ordinary weeping. φίλη τροφός 'dear nurse' names Eurycleia's role directly for the first time in this part (she was until now only ταμίη 'housekeeper'). ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the fixed formula 'spoke winged words', introducing her lament at 363.

sentences.t:
τίπτε δέ τοι, φίλε τέκνον, ἐνὶ φρεσὶ τοῦτο νόημα
ἔπλετο;
sentences.l:
Why ever, then, dear child, in your mind has this thought
arisen?
sentences.i: Why ever, dear child, has this notion come into your mind?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε contracted, 'why ever, what in the world'. τοι is the enclitic ethical dative, 'I tell you, mark you' — not the possessive 'your'. φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν, the seat of thought, in the Homeric -σι ending (Attic φρεσίν). ἔπλετο, from the defective verb πέλομαι 'come to be, happen', is an unaugmented aorist, one more instance of the pattern flagged at 321.

sentences.t:
πῇ δ’ ἐθέλεις ἰέναι πολλὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν
μοῦνος ἐὼν ἀγαπητός;
sentences.l:
And where do you wish to go, over much land,
being an only and cherished son?
sentences.i: Where do you mean to go, wandering over so much land, you who are an only and cherished son?
sentences.n: μοῦνος is the Ionic/epic form of μόνος 'alone, only'; ἀγαπητός, 'beloved, cherished', is the standard early epithet for an only child, marking how precious and vulnerable Telemachus is as Penelope's one son. ἐών is the uncontracted present participle of εἰμί (Attic ὤν).

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ὤλετο τηλόθι πάτρης
διογενὴς Ὀδυσεὺς ἀλλογνώτῳ ἐνὶ δήμῳ.
sentences.l:
But he has perished, far from his fatherland,
Zeus-sprung Odysseus, among a people unknown.
sentences.i: For he has perished, far from his own country, Zeus-born Odysseus, among a people that know him not.
sentences.n: ὤλετο is another unaugmented aorist (root aorist of ὄλλυμι, 'perished'), and τηλόθι πάτρης uses the suffix -θι 'at, in' with a genitive of place, 'far off from his native land' (compare Ἰθάκηνδε, -δε 'to', and Σπάρτηθεν, -θεν 'from', in this same part). διογενής repeats the new epithet from 352 for Odysseus, in Eurycleia's own mournful certainty that he is dead. ἀλλογνώτῳ, 'of another, unrecognized kind' (ἄλλος + γιγνώσκω), together with δῆμος 'land, people', pictures Odysseus perishing unknown, among strangers who could not have identified him.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ τοι αὐτίκ’ ἰόντι κακὰ φράσσονται ὀπίσσω,
ὥς κε δόλῳ φθίῃς, τάδε δ’ αὐτοὶ πάντα δάσονται.
sentences.l:
And they, I tell you, for you going forthwith, evils are plotting afterward,
so that by treachery you may perish, and these things all they themselves will divide up.
sentences.i: They, mind you, are already plotting evil for you against the time you are gone, so that you may die by treachery, and they may divide up all this wealth among themselves.
sentences.n: φράσσονται is a future middle of φράζομαι 'devise, plot' (distinct from the active φράζω 'point out, tell'). αὐτίκ' ἰόντι is a dative participle agreeing with an unexpressed 'you' (Telemachus), 'for you, the moment you have gone'. φθίῃς is an aorist subjunctive of φθίνω 'perish, waste away' in a purpose clause with ὥς κε. δάσονται, future of δατέομαι, echoes the same verb already used of the suitors' plan to divide Telemachus's goods among themselves (335).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μέν’ αὖθ’ ἐπὶ σοῖσι καθήμενος·
sentences.l: But stay here still, sitting among your own possessions;
sentences.i: No, stay here instead, sitting quietly among your own possessions;
sentences.n: μέν' is the imperative μένε, elided; αὖθι (here αὖθ') is 'here, on the spot', distinct from αὖτε/αὖ 'again, in turn' seen elsewhere in this part. σοῖσι is the possessive adjective 'your own' (σός), dative plural with ἐπί, 'over your own goods'; καθήμενος, from κάθημαι, is 'sitting, remaining seated' — Eurycleia's plea is that Telemachus stay safely at home rather than risk the sea.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον κακὰ πάσχειν οὐδ’ ἀλάλησθαι.
sentences.l:
Nor is there any need for you
upon the unharvested open-sea evils to suffer, nor to wander.
sentences.i: there is no need for you to suffer hardship on the unharvested sea, or to go wandering.
sentences.n: χρή is the impersonal 'it is needful', with σε as its subject-accusative and the infinitives πάσχειν and ἀλάλησθαι as what is (not) needed. ἀτρύγετος, 'unharvested' (of the sea), is the same disputed epithet already fixed for ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο; here it qualifies πόντον instead of ἅλς, and the rendering is kept the same regardless of which noun for 'sea' it modifies. ἀλάλησθαι is a perfect infinitive of ἀλάομαι 'wander' (the same verb used of Odysseus at 333), with perfect force shading into a simple present, 'to be a wanderer'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole line and its English are identical to the fixed reply-formula already published at 1.213, 1.230 and 1.306: αὖ marks the change of speaker, and πεπνυμένος, 'prudent', is kept for Telemachus wherever this formula recurs.

sentences.t: θάρσει, μαῖ’, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι ἄνευ θεοῦ ἥδε γε βουλή.
sentences.l: Take courage, nurse, since not, I tell you, without a god is this plan, at least.
sentences.i: Take heart, nurse — this plan of mine, be sure, is not without a god's help.
sentences.n: θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω 'be bold, take courage', a common opening to reassurance in Homer. τοι is again the ethical dative, 'mark you, I tell you' (as at 363), not a possessive. ἄνευ with the genitive θεοῦ is 'without a god'; γε underlines ἥδε βουλή, 'this plan of mine, at any rate'. Telemachus does not yet say which god; Athena, disguised as Mentes, set the journey in motion earlier in the book.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὄμοσον μὴ μητρὶ φίλῃ τάδε μυθήσασθαι,
πρίν γ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἑνδεκάτη τε δυωδεκάτη τε γένηται,
ἢ αὐτὴν ποθέσαι καὶ ἀφορμηθέντος ἀκοῦσαι,
ὡς ἂν μὴ κλαίουσα κατὰ χρόα καλὸν ἰάπτῃ.
sentences.l:
But swear not to my dear mother these things to tell,
until, at least, the eleventh day and the twelfth shall come,
or she herself should miss me and hear that I have set out,
so that, weeping, she may not mar her fair skin.
sentences.i: But swear not to tell my dear mother of this, until the eleventh or twelfth day has come, or until she misses me herself and hears that I am gone, so that she may not spoil her fair complexion with weeping.
sentences.n: ὄμοσον is the aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι 'swear'. πρίν γ' ὅτ' ἂν ... γένηται is a temporal clause with the subjunctive, 'until ... shall come'; ἑνδεκάτη and δυωδεκάτη understand ἡμέρα, '[day]'. ποθέσαι, from ποθέω 'long for, miss', and ἀφορμηθέντος, an aorist participle of ἀφορμάομαι 'set out, depart' (genitive absolute, unexpressed subject 'I'), give the two ways word might reach her — her own noticing, or a report. ἰάπτῃ, from ἰάπτω 'assail, mar', with κατὰ χρόα καλόν 'down her fair skin', pictures grief physically damaging a woman's complexion.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, γρῆυς δὲ θεῶν μέγαν ὅρκον ἀπώμνυ.
sentences.l: So then he spoke, and the old woman swore the gods' great oath.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old woman swore a great oath by the gods.
sentences.n: ἄρα inside ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is a variant of the plain ὣς ἔφατο/ἔφη formula, adding a light inferential nuance, 'so then'. γρῆυς is the epic form of γραῦς 'old woman' (nominative singular), used here instead of a name, since Telemachus has just called her μαῖα. ἀπώμνυ is an unaugmented imperfect of ἀπόμνυμι 'swear (solemnly)', with θεῶν as an objective-feeling genitive, 'an oath by the gods', and ὅρκον as its cognate object.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσέν τε τελεύτησέν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτά οἱ οἶνον ἐν ἀμφιφορεῦσιν ἄφυσσεν,
ἐν δέ οἱ ἄλφιτα χεῦεν ἐϋρραφέεσσι δοροῖσι.
sentences.l:
But when then she had sworn and finished the oath,
at once then for him wine into jars she drew off,
and in for him barley-meal she poured, into well-sewn skin-bags.
sentences.i: And when she had sworn and completed the oath, at once she drew off wine for him into jars, and poured barley-meal into well-stitched skin-bags.
sentences.n: τελεύτησεν τὸν ὅρκον, 'brought the oath to completion', pairs with ὄμοσεν to mark not just the swearing but its formal fulfilment. This passage restates Telemachus's own orders at 349 and 354 almost word for word, now as accomplished fact — a typically Homeric way of confirming that an instruction has been carried out exactly. οἱ is again the enclitic dative 'for him'.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἐς δώματ’ ἰὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμίλει.
sentences.l: But Telemachus, to the halls going, with the suitors mingled.
sentences.i: Telemachus meanwhile went back to the hall and mixed with the suitors.
sentences.n: ὁμίλει, imperfect of ὁμιλέω 'consort, mingle with', takes the dative μνηστῆρσιν; the imperfect suggests he simply rejoined their company, giving nothing away of his plan. ἰών is the present participle of εἶμι 'go'.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else.
sentences.n: ἐνόησε, aorist of νοέω 'perceive, have in mind, devise', here means 'contrived, thought up'; ἄλλο is its object, 'another thing' — this exact line recurs verbatim at 393, marking a second, parallel initiative of Athena's within the same stretch, and both units carry the identical English the repeated-line rule requires. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is the fixed epithet, 'gleaming-eyed Athena'.

sentences.t:
Τηλεμάχῳ ἐικυῖα κατὰ πτόλιν ᾤχετο πάντῃ,
καί ῥα ἑκάστῳ φωτὶ παρισταμένη φάτο μῦθον,
ἑσπερίους δ’ ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν ἀγέρεσθαι ἀνώγει.
sentences.l:
Likened to Telemachus, throughout the city she went everywhere,
and, standing beside each man, she spoke a word,
and bade them, at evening, upon the swift ship to gather.
sentences.i: Taking the likeness of Telemachus, she went everywhere throughout the city, and stood by each man and spoke to him, telling them to gather at evening aboard the swift ship.
sentences.n: ἐικυῖα is the perfect participle of ἔοικα 'be like, resemble', with the dative Τηλεμάχῳ, 'like to Telemachus'; this part uses the same disguise idea again at 401, where Athena takes the shape of Mentor instead. πτόλις is the older epic by-form of πόλις. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone, go about'. ἑσπερίους, though it agrees grammatically with the implied 'them' (the crew), functions adverbially, 'in the evening'; ἀνώγει, from the defective verb ἄνωγα, means 'commanded, bade' and regularly takes an infinitive, here ἀγέρεσθαι 'to gather' (from ἀγείρω).

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αὖτε Φρονίοιο Νοήμονα φαίδιμον υἱὸν
ᾔτεε νῆα θοήν·
sentences.l:
And she, in turn, Noemon, the shining son of Phronius,
asked for a swift ship;
sentences.i: And she went and asked Noemon, the shining son of Phronius, for a swift ship;
sentences.n: Φρονίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic Φρονίου), and φαίδιμος 'shining, glorious' is a common heroic epithet for a young man of good family. ᾔτεε is an imperfect of αἰτέω 'ask for, request'. Noemon appears here as a minor Ithacan who lends Telemachus his ship, giving his consent to what he takes to be an ordinary request from Telemachus himself, not knowing the god behind it.

sentences.t: ὁ δέ οἱ πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο.
sentences.l: And he, to her, readily agreed.
sentences.i: and he readily agreed.
sentences.n: πρόφρων, literally 'forward-minded, eager', is used adverbially of a willing, ready assent. ὑπέδεκτο, aorist middle of ὑποδέχομαι 'undertake, promise', shows Noemon giving his consent without hesitation or suspicion.

sentences.t:
δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί,
καὶ τότε νῆα θοὴν ἅλαδ’ εἴρυσε, πάντα δ’ ἐν αὐτῇ
ὅπλ’ ἐτίθει, τά τε νῆες ἐύσσελμοι φορέουσι.
sentences.l:
And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy,
and then the swift ship to the sea she drew, and all within it
the gear she was placing, which well-benched ships carry.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark, and then she drew the swift ship down to the sea, and began stowing in it all the gear that well-benched ships carry.
sentences.n: δύσετο is an unaugmented aorist middle of δύω 'set, sink' (of the sun). σκιόωντο is a diectasis form, the contracted -οῦντο stretched back out to -όωντο to fit the verse, from σκιάω/σκιόω 'cast a shadow, darken' — the same artificial lengthening seen in αἰτιόωνται-type forms. ἅλαδ' carries the -δε suffix, 'seaward'. The unnamed subject of εἴρυσε and ἐτίθει is most naturally Athena, still disguised as Telemachus, continuing her stage-management of the whole departure. ἐύσσελμος 'well-benched' (of a ship with good rowing-benches) is a standing epithet, and τε in the relative clause marks a general truth about ships of this kind.

sentences.t:
στῆσε δ’ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῇ λιμένος, περὶ δ’ ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι
ἁθρόοι ἠγερέθοντο·
sentences.l:
And she moored it at the edge of the harbor, and around, the noble comrades
were gathering together in a body;
sentences.i: She moored it at the edge of the harbor, and the noble comrades gathered round it in a body;
sentences.n: στῆσε is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι, 'she stationed, made to stand' (the ship), as opposed to the intransitive ἕστασαν already seen at 341. ἠγερέθοντο is an imperfect passive of ἀγείρω 'gather', ἁθρόοι 'in a body' repeating the adjective already used of the stored treasure. ἐσχατιή is literally 'the furthest point, edge', here of the harbor.

sentences.t: θεὰ δ’ ὤτρυνεν ἕκαστον.
sentences.l: And the goddess urged each one on.
sentences.i: and the goddess urged them on, one by one.
sentences.n: ὤτρυνεν, imperfect of ὀτρύνω 'urge on, spur', is the same verb that will describe Telemachus's own exhortation to his crew at 422 — the disguised Athena and the true Telemachus are given the identical verb of leadership.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else.
sentences.n: The line repeats 382 exactly, and its English repeats with it, as the rule for a recurring line requires: Athena's first idea sent Noemon's ship to the harbor; her second, that follows here, will put the suitors to sleep and fetch Telemachus himself.

sentences.t: βῆ ῥ’ ἰέναι πρὸς δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο·
sentences.l: She set out to go to the halls of divine Odysseus;
sentences.i: She set out for the halls of divine Odysseus;
sentences.n: βῆ ... ἰέναι is a variant of the fixed 'set out to go' formula (elsewhere βῆ δ'/βῆ ῥ' ἴμεν, with the older infinitive ἴμεν; here the newer ἰέναι appears instead, both from the same verb εἶμι). θείοιο, a genitive in -οιο, is the word already fixed as 'divine' for Phemius the minstrel; it is applied to Odysseus here, and the rendering is kept the same regardless of whose name it qualifies, while staying distinct from δῖος 'heavenly' (also of Odysseus, e.g. 342) and ἀντίθεος 'godlike'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μνηστήρεσσιν ἐπὶ γλυκὺν ὕπνον ἔχευε,
πλάζε δὲ πίνοντας, χειρῶν δ’ ἔκβαλλε κύπελλα.
sentences.l:
There upon the suitors sweet sleep she poured,
and made them stagger as they drank, and from their hands cast down the cups.
sentences.i: There she poured sweet sleep over the suitors, and made them stagger as they drank, and knocked the cups from their hands.
sentences.n: ἔχευε is an unaugmented imperfect of χέω 'pour' (the same verb behind χεῦον/χεῦεν at 354 and 380, there of barley-meal, here of sleep). πλάζε, imperfect of πλάζω 'make to wander, confound', is the same verb as πλάγχθη in the poem's opening line, though here concretely, 'made them reel'. ἔκβαλλε is imperfect of ἐκβάλλω, with χειρῶν as a genitive of separation, 'out of their hands'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ εὕδειν ὤρνυντο κατὰ πτόλιν, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
ἥατ’, ἐπεί σφισιν ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔπιπτεν.
sentences.l:
And they rose to go to sleep throughout the city, nor indeed any longer
were sitting, since upon them sleep on their eyelids was falling.
sentences.i: And they got up to go to bed, each to his own house in the city, and no longer stayed sitting there, since sleep was falling on their eyelids.
sentences.n: ὤρνυντο is an imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι 'stir, rouse'; with the infinitive εὕδειν, 'bestirred themselves to sleep'. ἥατο (here ἥατ') is a 3rd plural imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit' with the Homeric ending -ατο (Attic ἧντο), the same verb recurring as ἥατ' at 403. σφισιν is the epic dative plural pronoun 'to/for them' (= αὐτοῖς), and βλεφάροισι(ν) is another dative plural in -οισι(ν).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχον προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
ἐκπροκαλεσσαμένη μεγάρων ἐὺ ναιεταόντων,
Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν·
sentences.l:
But gleaming-eyed Athena addressed Telemachus,
having called him forth from the halls well-inhabited,
likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice:
sentences.i: But gleaming-eyed Athena spoke to Telemachus, calling him out from the well-inhabited halls, having taken the shape of Mentor, in body and in voice alike:
sentences.n: προσέφη ... γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη has Τηλέμαχον as its object, not its subject: Athena addresses Telemachus, though the accusative precedes the nominative in the Greek order. ἐκπροκαλεσσαμένη is a compound aorist participle (ἐκ- + προ- + καλέομαι), 'having called out from', with μεγάρων ... ναιεταόντων an uncontracted genitive phrase, 'from the well-peopled halls'. Μέντορι εἰδομένη ἠμὲν δέμας ἠδὲ καὶ αὐδήν repeats, word for word, the line already published at 2.268 (odyssey-007), where it described the same disguise; its l ('likened to Mentor, both in body and in voice') is reused here unchanged, adapted only in its final punctuation to the colon this speech-introduction needs. εἰδομένη is technically a present-participle spelling doing service as an aorist, a known quirk of εἴδομαι already flagged in the shipped glossary.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἤδη μέν τοι ἐυκνήμιδες ἑταῖροι
ἥατ’ ἐπήρετμοι τὴν σὴν ποτιδέγμενοι ὁρμήν·
sentences.l:
Telemachus, already, I tell you, your well-greaved comrades
are sitting, oar in hand, awaiting your setting-out;
sentences.i: Telemachus, your well-greaved comrades are already sitting at their oars, waiting for you to give the signal to set out;
sentences.n: ἐυκνήμιδες is the adjective already fixed as 'well-greaved' for the Achaeans generally (ἐυκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί); here it describes Telemachus's own crew instead, and the rendering stays the same regardless of whom it describes. ἥατ' is again the Homeric ἧμαι-imperfect seen at 398. ἐπήρετμοι, 'at the oar', describes men already seated and ready to row. ποτιδέγμενοι is ποτι- (= προσ-) + δέγμενος, the participle of δέχομαι 'await, expect', governing ὁρμήν 'the start, the setting-out' as its object.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν, μὴ δηθὰ διατρίβωμεν ὁδοῖο.
sentences.l: But let us go, let us not for long delay from our way.
sentences.i: Come, let us go; let us not put off our journey any longer.
sentences.n: ἴομεν is a hortatory subjunctive of εἶμι, 'let us go'. διατρίβωμεν, from διατρίβω 'wear away time, linger', takes ὁδοῖο (another genitive in -οιο) as a genitive of separation, 'delay from the road', i.e. 'hold up our departure'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ ἡγήσατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
καρπαλίμως·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, Pallas Athena led the way,
swiftly;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Pallas Athena led the way swiftly;
sentences.n: φωνήσασα is the aorist participle of φωνέω 'utter, speak aloud' (distinct from φημί, used more of the bare act of speaking than of its content). ἡγήσατο, from ἡγέομαι 'lead the way', takes no object here; the person led follows from context at 406. καρπαλίμως 'swiftly, nimbly' is a common adverb of quick divine or heroic movement.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα μετ’ ἴχνια βαῖνε θεοῖο.
sentences.l: And he then walked following in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.i: and he followed close behind in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.n: μετ' ... βαῖνε is tmesis for μετέβαινε, 'walked after, followed', with ἴχνια 'footprints, tracks' as its object and θεοῖο ('of the god', another -οιο genitive) referring to Athena — grammatically masculine because she is disguised as Mentor, a man. Telemachus follows what he takes to be an old family friend, not knowing it is the goddess herself.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλυθον ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
εὗρον ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ θινὶ κάρη κομόωντας ἑταίρους.
sentences.l:
But when then they had come down to the ship and the sea,
they found then upon the shore the long-haired-of-head comrades.
sentences.i: And when they had come down to the ship and the sea, they found the long-haired comrades there upon the shore.
sentences.n: κατήλυθον is an unaugmented aorist of κατέρχομαι, 'came down'. κάρη κομόωντας, literally 'long-haired as to the head', is the fixed epithet elsewhere applied to 'the Achaeans' as a people; here it qualifies 'comrades' instead, and the same English, 'the long-haired', is kept regardless of the noun it modifies.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειφ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.l: And to them then spoke the sacred force of Telemachus:
sentences.i: And the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus spoke to them:
sentences.n: μετέειπε ('spoke among them', from μετά + εἶπον) is elided and aspirated to μετέειφ' before the rough breathing of ἱερή. ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, literally 'the sacred strength of Telemachus', is a periphrasis: Homer regularly names a hero by his ἲς 'force, might' plus his name in the genitive, in place of the bare name, much as βίη Ἡρακληείη names Heracles by his 'strength'. This is a new fixed rendering for this part (see new-renderings.md), since the same periphrasis is likely to recur for other figures later in the poem.

sentences.t: δεῦτε, φίλοι, ἤια φερώμεθα·
sentences.l: Come, friends, let us carry the provisions;
sentences.i: Come, friends, let us bring the stores aboard;
sentences.n: δεῦτε is the plural imperative of an old verb of motion, used as a bare interjection, 'come!' (singular δεῦρο). ἤια is a plural noun for 'provisions, stores for a journey'. φερώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive middle, 'let us carry/fetch for ourselves'.

sentences.t:
πάντα γὰρ ἤδη
ἁθρό’ ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ.
sentences.l:
for everything already
lies gathered in the hall.
sentences.i: for everything is already gathered together in the hall.
sentences.n: The verb 'is/lies' is left unexpressed, as often with ἐστί in Homer; ἁθρόα, 'gathered in a heap', is the same adjective already used of the treasure-room's stores and the assembled comrades earlier in this part.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ δ’ ἐμὴ οὔ τι πέπυσται,
οὐδ’ ἄλλαι δμωαί, μία δ’ οἴη μῦθον ἄκουσεν.
sentences.l:
And my mother has not at all learned of it,
nor the other slave-women, but one alone heard the word.
sentences.i: My mother knows nothing of it at all, nor do the other slave-women — only one alone has heard the news.
sentences.n: πέπυσται is a perfect of πυνθάνομαι, 'has learned, has got word of', with lasting force: she remains ignorant even now. δμωαί, 'female slaves, bondwomen', are the household servants generally, of whom Eurycleia is one but of higher standing; μία ... οἴη 'one alone' picks her out without naming her again, since she was sworn to secrecy at 373.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο, τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο.
sentences.l: So then having spoken, he led the way, and they together followed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way, and they followed along together.
sentences.n: This line pairs with 405 (ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ' ἡγήσατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη), now with the masculine participle φωνήσας for Telemachus himself leading his own men, rather than Athena leading him. τοί is again the pronoun 'they' (the comrades), and ἕποντο is an imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', with ἅμα 'together, at the same time'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντα φέροντες ἐυσσέλμῳ ἐπὶ νηὶ
κάτθεσαν, ὡς ἐκέλευσεν Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός.
sentences.l:
And they then, carrying everything, upon the well-benched ship
stowed it, as Odysseus' dear son commanded.
sentences.i: And they carried everything aboard and stowed it on the well-benched ship, just as Odysseus' dear son had ordered.
sentences.n: κάτθεσαν is a syncopated, unaugmented aorist of κατατίθημι, 'stowed, set down' (= κατέθηκαν). ἐυσσέλμῳ, 'well-benched', is the same epithet already applied to Noemon's ship. Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός, 'Odysseus' dear son', is the already-fixed periphrasis for Telemachus.

sentences.t:
ἂν δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος νηὸς βαῖν’, ἦρχε δ’ Ἀθήνη,
νηὶ δ’ ἐνὶ πρυμνῇ κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο·
sentences.l:
And then Telemachus went aboard the ship, and Athena led the way,
and in the ship, at the stern, then she sat down;
sentences.i: Then Telemachus climbed aboard the ship, with Athena going first, and she sat down in the stern of the ship;
sentences.n: ἂν ... βαῖνε is tmesis for ἀνέβαινε, 'went up, embarked', with νηός a genitive of the goal, 'onto the ship' (an unusual case with a verb of motion). ἦρχε, from ἄρχω, here means 'went first, led the way' rather than 'ruled'. κατ' ... ἕζετο is tmesis for καθέζετο, 'sat down', unaugmented; πρυμνή is the stern, the seat of honour and command in a Homeric ship.

sentences.t:
ἄγχι δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῆς
ἕζετο Τηλέμαχος.
sentences.l:
And then close beside her
sat down Telemachus.
sentences.i: and Telemachus sat down close beside her.
sentences.n: ἄγχι, 'near, close by', with the genitive αὐτῆς, 'to her', places Telemachus deliberately near the disguised goddess. ἕζετο is the plain imperfect middle of ἕζομαι 'sit down', without the preverb κατά as in the line before, since no compound is needed for the simple act of sitting.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ πρυμνήσι’ ἔλυσαν,
ἂν δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βάντες ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον.
sentences.l:
And they loosed the stern-cables,
and they themselves too, having gone aboard, upon the rowing-benches were sitting down.
sentences.i: And they cast off the stern-cables, and climbed aboard themselves and sat down at the oarlocks.
sentences.n: πρυμνήσια are the cables mooring the ship's stern to shore. ἂν ... βάντες is tmesis for ἀναβάντες, 'having gone up, embarked' (the same compound as ἀνέβαινε at 416). κληῖσι, dative plural of κληΐς, are the thole-pins or benches at which the oarsmen sit — a different word from κληϊστός 'closing' seen at 344, though visually similar.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
ἀκραῆ Ζέφυρον, κελάδοντ’ ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον.
sentences.l:
And for them a favorable wind sent gleaming-eyed Athena,
the fresh West Wind, sounding over the wine-faced open-sea.
sentences.i: And gleaming-eyed Athena sent them a favoring wind, the fresh West Wind, singing over the sea that has the look of wine.
sentences.n: ἵει is an imperfect of ἵημι 'send, let go', with τοῖσιν a dative of advantage, 'for them'. ἴκμενος οὖρος 'a favorable, following wind' is a formula for fair sailing weather. ἀκραής describes a wind blowing keen and fresh. οἴνοπα πόντον is the already-fixed 'wine-faced open-sea' (the literal image kept rather than the conventional 'wine-dark', whose sense is not actually what οἶνοψ says); κελάδοντα, 'sounding, roaring', personifies the wind's noise over the water.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσεν
ὅπλων ἅπτεσθαι·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus, having urged on his comrades, commanded them
to lay hold of the tackle;
sentences.i: And Telemachus urged his comrades on and ordered them to take hold of the ship's gear;
sentences.n: ἐποτρύνας, an aorist participle of ὀτρύνω (the same verb as ὤτρυνεν at 392, now of Telemachus himself), governs the dative ἑτάροισιν, 'having roused his comrades'. ὅπλων ἅπτεσθαι, 'to take hold of the tackle', uses ἅπτομαι with the genitive, its regular construction; ὅπλα here are the ship's gear and rigging, not weapons.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ὀτρύνοντος ἄκουσαν.
sentences.l: And they heeded him urging.
sentences.i: and they obeyed his command.
sentences.n: ἀκούω here takes the genitive of the person heard (ὀτρύνοντος, 'him urging'), a different construction from ἀκούσω 'I may hear [something]' at 360, which took the thing heard; the genitive construction with ἀκούω regularly marks the person, not the thing, heard.

sentences.t:
ἱστὸν δ’ εἰλάτινον κοίλης ἔντοσθε μεσόδμης
στῆσαν ἀείραντες, κατὰ δὲ προτόνοισιν ἔδησαν,
ἕλκον δ’ ἱστία λευκὰ ἐυστρέπτοισι βοεῦσιν.
sentences.l:
And the mast, of fir, within the hollow mast-block
they set up, having raised it, and down with the forestays they bound it,
and they hauled up the white sails with well-twisted oxhide ropes.
sentences.i: They raised the fir mast and set it in the hollow mast-block, and made it fast with the forestays, and hauled up the white sails with well-twisted ropes of oxhide.
sentences.n: εἰλάτινος, 'of fir, of pine', describes the wood the mast is made from. μεσόδμη is the crossbeam or block amidships that holds the mast's foot. κατὰ ... ἔδησαν is tmesis for κατέδησαν, 'bound down, made fast'; προτόνοισι, dative plural in -οισι, are the forestays that brace the mast forward. ἐυστρέπτοισι, 'well-twisted', and βοεῦσιν, 'of ox-hide', describe the rope, twisted leather being the ordinary cordage of an early ship.

sentences.t:
ἔπρησεν δ’ ἄνεμος μέσον ἱστίον, ἀμφὶ δὲ κῦμα
στείρῃ πορφύρεον μεγάλ’ ἴαχε νηὸς ἰούσης·
sentences.l:
And the wind filled the middle of the sail, and around, the wave,
at the stem, surging, loudly resounded, as the ship went on;
sentences.i: And the wind filled the belly of the sail, and the surging wave roared loudly about the stem as the ship went on her way;
sentences.n: ἔπρησεν, from πίμπρημι/πρήθω 'blow, swell', describes the wind bellying out the sail. στεῖρα is the ship's stem or cutwater, the point that cuts the water; πορφύρεον, literally 'dark-gleaming, surging' (the same root that gives 'purple'), describes the churn of water there, not a colour. ἴαχε, from ἰάχω 'cry out, resound', is used of a loud natural noise. νηὸς ἰούσης is a genitive absolute, 'as the ship went'.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἔθεεν κατὰ κῦμα διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθον.
sentences.l: And she sped on over the wave, accomplishing her way.
sentences.i: And the ship ran on over the waves, making her way through.
sentences.n: ἔθεεν is an imperfect of θέω 'run'. διαπρήσσουσα κέλευθον, 'making her way through', uses διαπράσσω in the sense of covering or completing a course, a formula for swift sea-travel; κέλευθος 'path, way' returns at 434 to close the part.

sentences.t:
δησάμενοι δ’ ἄρα ὅπλα θοὴν ἀνὰ νῆα μέλαιναν
στήσαντο κρητῆρας ἐπιστεφέας οἴνοιο,
λεῖβον δ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσιν,
ἐκ πάντων δὲ μάλιστα Διὸς γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ.
sentences.l:
And having made fast the tackle then, throughout the swift black ship
they set up mixing-bowls brimming with wine,
and poured libations to the immortal gods who are forever-born,
and of all, most of all, to the gleaming-eyed daughter of Zeus.
sentences.i: And having made the tackle fast throughout the swift black ship, they set up bowls brimming with wine and poured libations to the immortal, everlasting gods, and above all the rest to the gleaming-eyed daughter of Zeus.
sentences.n: δησάμενοι, aorist middle participle of δέω 'bind, make fast', picks up the rigging just finished. ἐπιστεφής, 'crowned, heaped to the brim', describes a bowl filled full for libation. αἰειγενέτῃσιν, 'ever-born, everlasting' (αἰεί + γίγνομαι), is a distinct epithet from the already-fixed θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες 'the gods who are forever' (ἐόντες 'being', not 'born'), and is kept as its own literal rendering rather than folded into that formula (see new-renderings.md). Διὸς γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ, 'the gleaming-eyed daughter of Zeus', is Athena again, honoured above all the gods since she is the one guiding this voyage, though the crew do not know it.

sentences.t: παννυχίη μέν ῥ’ ἥ γε καὶ ἠῶ πεῖρε κέλευθον.
sentences.l: All night long, then, she indeed, even into the dawn, kept cutting through her path.
sentences.i: All night long, and on into the dawn, the ship cut steadily through her course.
sentences.n: παννυχίη, 'all through the night', is an adjective agreeing with the ship (ἥ γε, 'she'), used adverbially of time, as ἑσπέριος was at 357. πεῖρε, imperfect of πείρω 'pierce, drive through', with κέλευθον as a cognate-type object, 'cut her way'; ἠῶ is the accusative of extent, 'on into the dawn'. The part ends with the ship still under way, the crew's landfall left for the next stretch of the poem.
